cookie-marshmallow-and-peanut-butter-wit.title: Cookie, Marshmallow and Peanut Butter with Oat Cereal, No‑Bake

content.title: About
content.content: A ready‑to‑eat no‑bake snack made from soft cookie pieces, fluffy marshmallow, rich peanut butter and crunchy oat cereal. The ingredients are mixed, pressed into bars and chilled until set.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The combination of cookie and marshmallow creates a contrast of chewiness and sweetness.
Peanut butter adds a deep nutty flavor and heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats.
Oat cereal boosts fiber content and gives a satisfying crunch.
No‑bake preparation preserves heat‑sensitive vitamins better than baking.
Ideal for a quick snack or post‑workout energy bar.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Peanut butter and oat cereal provide plant‑based protein that supports muscle repair.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats from peanut butter promote cardiovascular health.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Oats contribute soluble fiber, aiding digestion and satiety.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Oats and peanuts supply thiamine, niacin and folate, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Marshmallow often includes vanilla, and peanut butter provides vitamin E, both acting as antioxidants.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: The product contains peanut butter, which can trigger severe allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Rich in fats and sugars, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Marshmallow and cookie add simple sugars that may raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Gluten presence
items.content: If the cookie contains wheat, the snack is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut the bars into bite‑size pieces and enjoy as a standalone snack or add to yogurt, ice cream or fruit salad. For a firmer texture, chill the bars briefly in the refrigerator.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 5 days or refrigerate for up to 2 weeks. For longer storage, freeze to prevent peanut butter from going rancid.

content.title: About
content.content: Corn, scalloped or pudding is a dish made from whole corn kernels, milk, eggs and sugar, baked until a golden crust forms. In the United States it is often served in the autumn season and is considered a traditional family comfort food in many regions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn is one of the oldest cultivated crops, domesticated over 7,000 years ago in Mesoamerica.
The baked version is commonly called “corn pudding” or “corn casserole” in English‑speaking countries.
Traditional recipes include milk, cream, and sometimes butter, giving the dish a rich, silky texture.
In some U.S. regions the pudding is served with maple syrup or cinnamon for extra flavor.
Corn’s bright yellow color comes from carotenoids, which have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Corn provides carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Source of magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals help regulate blood pressure and support muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Carotenoids and phenolic compounds in corn protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn, ranging from skin rashes to severe symptoms.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Traditional pudding often contains added sugar, which may be unsuitable for people with diabetes or those limiting calories.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: The dish is rich in fats and carbs, so portion control is advisable to avoid over‑consumption.

items.title: Gluten in additives
items.content: Some recipes use flour or starch that contain gluten; gluten‑free alternatives should be used for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn pudding can be served warm as a dessert or side dish. Bake it in a casserole dish and enjoy with berry sauce, whipped cream, or ice cream. A chilled version is also refreshing in summer.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared pudding in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in the microwave or oven as needed. Do not keep at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Guava (Psidium guajava) is a tropical fruit native to Mexico, Central America, and northern South America, with thin green-to-yellow skin and sweet, fragrant, white, pink, or red flesh full of small hard seeds. It has a flavor between pear and strawberry. Guava is eaten fresh and used in juices, jams, desserts, and savory sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Guava is one of the richest fruit sources of vitamin C, with more per serving than oranges.
The skin, flesh, and seeds are all edible, though the seeds are hard.
Pink-fleshed guavas get their color from lycopene, the same pigment found in tomatoes.
Guava has a strong, sweet, musky fragrance when ripe.
Guava leaves are also used to make teas in some traditions.

items.title: Very rich in vitamin C
items.content: Guava provides more vitamin C than most fruits, supporting the immune system and skin.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Guava is one of the higher-fiber fruits, which supports digestion and fullness.

items.title: Contains lycopene and carotenoids
items.content: Pink guavas provide lycopene and carotenoids with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Provides potassium and folate
items.content: These nutrients support normal blood pressure and cell function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Guava is relatively low in calories for its nutrient content.

items.title: Hard seeds
items.content: The small hard seeds can be hard on teeth and can cause constipation or discomfort in large amounts. Young children should not eat them whole.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Eating a lot of guava may cause gas or bloating in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Blood sugar medication
items.content: Guava, especially guava leaf extracts, may lower blood sugar. People taking diabetes medication should consult a healthcare professional before using concentrated products.

items.title: Allergic reactions and residues
items.content: Guava allergy is uncommon but can occur, and the fruit should be washed thoroughly before eating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Guava can be eaten fresh with the skin on, sliced into fruit salads, blended into juices and smoothies, or cooked into jams, jellies, and sauces. In some countries it is eaten with a sprinkle of salt or chili. Remove the seeds if you prefer a smoother texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep firm guavas at room temperature until they soften and smell sweet. Ripe guavas can be refrigerated for a few days. Cut guava should be stored in an airtight container and eaten within a couple of days. The pulp can be frozen.

content.title: About
content.content: Pineapple (Ananas comosus) is a tropical fruit native to South America. It has a sweet-tart flavor, juicy fragrant flesh, and a tough, spiky skin. Pineapple is eaten fresh, canned, or as juice, and is added to desserts, salads, baked goods, and meat dishes, or grilled.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A pineapple is not a single fruit but a multiple fruit formed from many fused berries.
It grows not on a tree but on a low plant close to the ground.
Pineapple contains bromelain, an enzyme that breaks down proteins, which is why fresh pineapple can make your mouth tingle.
Because of bromelain, gelatin made with raw pineapple does not set, while canned pineapple does not have this effect.
Pineapple does not become noticeably sweeter after harvest, so it is important to choose a ripe fruit.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains manganese
items.content: Manganese plays a role in metabolism and bone formation.

items.title: Contains bromelain
items.content: Bromelain is studied as a compound that may support digestion.

items.title: Contains fiber and water
items.content: Pineapple is refreshing and provides some fiber.

items.title: Contains B vitamins
items.content: It provides thiamine and vitamin B6, which help the body get energy from food.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Pineapple is acidic and may cause heartburn or irritate the mouth, tongue, and tooth enamel.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Pineapple allergy is possible, including reactions to bromelain.

items.title: Sugar
items.content: Pineapple contains natural sugars, so people with diabetes should watch their portion size.

items.title: Bromelain and medications
items.content: Large amounts of bromelain or bromelain supplements may interact with anticoagulants and some antibiotics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut off the top and base, slice away the skin, remove the "eyes," and, if you like, the tough core. Cut the flesh into slices or cubes and eat it fresh, add it to salads, smoothies, yogurt, and desserts, or grill it. Choose canned pineapple in its own juice rather than in syrup.

content.title: Storage
content.content: A whole pineapple can be kept at room temperature for one to two days, then moved to the refrigerator. Store cut pineapple in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3–5 days, or freeze it in pieces. Store canned pineapple as directed on the package, and refrigerate it after opening.

content.title: About
content.content: Soft pretzels are a yeast‑leavened baked snack formed into twisted knots, frozen immediately after shaping. After thawing they retain a tender, slightly chewy texture and a mildly salty flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soft pretzels originated in Central Europe, where they were traditionally shaped into knots.
Freezing locks in freshness and aroma without the need for preservatives.
In the United States they are often served with cheese sauce or mustard.
The classic recipe uses wheat flour, yeast, water, salt, and a touch of sugar.
There are flavored versions that include paprika, garlic, or other spices.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Pretzels provide complex carbs that give lasting satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many baked snacks, soft pretzels contain relatively little fat.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: The wheat flour supplies a modest amount of iron, important for blood formation.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 supports protein metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Convenient to prepare
items.content: Thawing and a short bake take only a few minutes, making them a quick snack.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Pretzels are made from wheat flour and are not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salt is added for flavor; those monitoring sodium intake should choose an unsalted version.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because the carbs are quickly absorbed, pretzels can raise blood sugar levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thaw at room temperature or in the microwave, then bake in a preheated oven for 5‑7 minutes until lightly golden. Serve as a snack on its own, with dips (cheese, mustard), or as a side to soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen pretzels in a sealed bag in the freezer at –18 °C. After thawing, consume within 2‑3 days and store in the refrigerator.

content.title: About
content.content: Snowpeas are frozen pea pods that have been pre‑cooked and contain no added fat. They retain the sweet flavor and crisp texture of fresh peas while being ready to heat and serve.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Snowpeas are often called “snow peas” because of their pale green color after freezing.
Heat processing locks in most B‑vitamins and vitamin C.
Freezing occurs immediately after harvest, preserving peak freshness.
Pea pods are a good source of plant protein and dietary fiber.
Snowpeas can be added directly to hot dishes without thawing.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: A serving provides about 5 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: No added fat makes it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Contains vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, iron, and magnesium, important for immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Phytonutrients in peas help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to pea family members.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain batches may be lightly salted; check the label if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Freezing‑related quality issues
items.content: Improper storage can cause ice crystal formation and degrade texture.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add Snowpeas to soups, stews, pasta, stir‑fries, or simply heat them as a side dish in the microwave or on a skillet. They also work well in salads after a quick sauté.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen Snowpeas in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once thawed, use within 2–3 days and do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
